blocks.label: Lecture introduction and overview
blocks.why: The lecturer welcomes the class and introduces the lecture's focus on the initiation and resolution of inflammation.
blocks.content: Hi, everyone. Can everyone hear me okay? Super. Welcome back to Biology of Disease. I'm Adrian Liston, and today we're going to be talking about the initiation and the resolution of inflammation. Now, today should be the day where you feel like you know all the bits of the immune system, and it's coming together. I'm not going to be introducing new concepts. I'm not going to be introducing new cell types, not really even new molecules. We're going to instead go deeper into the molecules and cells that have already been introduced, and we're showing how they can be put together in different ways to make immune reactions.

blocks.label: Recognition of infection via PAMPs and DAMPs
blocks.why: The lecturer explains how the innate immune system senses danger directly through microbial products and indirectly through cellular damage signals.
blocks.content: Now, the key to an immune reaction is, first of all, recognizing that there is an infection. As I mentioned last week, there's no intrinsic ability of the immune system to know that there is an infection going on. They need to have sensors that are in place in order to detect pathogens. So we have to have a mechanism by which cells know that they should be activated. There is no advantage to having these incredibly powerful immune machines that can destroy everything if they don't get activated at the right time and against the right target. So that process is known as recognition. Now, the innate immune system and the adaptive immune system, they fundamentally differ on how they are recognizing the presence of an infection. I'm going to be talking today about how the innate immune system recognizes infection, and the adaptive immune recognition, that'll take place in a few lectures time under a different lecturer. So how does the innate immune system recognize that there is an infection? And essentially, we have a set of receptors that are going to recognize PAMPs and DAMPs. So, what are PAMPs and DAMPs? PAMPs are pathogen-associated molecular patterns, and these are direct signals of an infection. They are direct products made by a microbe, and the host immune system has receptors that recognize that microbial product, and it's going to activate the immune system. So it is detecting the presence of products that should only be made by microbes, therefore they are pathogen-associated molecular patterns. Now, the immune system doesn't just have to rely on directly sensing microbial products. It can also indirectly sense the signs of an infection through damage-associated molecular patterns or DAMPs. And what DAMPs are, they are signals of cellular damage. They are signals that cells are being killed or damaged, that tissue is being destroyed. Now, if you have got cells mysteriously dying, that's a good sign that something is there killing them. And so the immune system is sensitive to signs of lots of cells dying or being killed off, even in the absence of directly seeing a microbial product. Has anyone here heard of mirror life? No? It's a concept that you could engineer life that has very similar properties, but all the chirality of the molecules are flipped, and the idea being that this life, these bacteria, mirror bacteria, would be invisible to our immune system because all of the molecules that they produce are flipped in their chirality and therefore they wouldn't bind our receptors. Now, even if we had mirror life, even if we had completely alien life forms that did not evolve from the last common ancestor, we went to colonize a planet in a galaxy far, far away, and there's a bacterial life there that had no relationship to us, and none of our receptors worked to recognize those pathogens, those microbes, we would still be able to detect the presence of an infection once those microbes started killing off our tissues. We would still detect a whole bunch of cells dying and becoming apoptotic and products being released from our cells just because of the damage itself. Okay? So we have the ability to detect damage apart from detecting the infection, and that's through the DAMPs as well as the PAMPs. So both PAMPs and DAMPs will trigger inflammation, and the key cells here are sentinel cells. So pretty much all cells in the body will have some type of PAMP or DAMP receptor, but the sentinel cells, mast cells, macrophages, dendritic cells, epithelial cells, these are particularly good at sensing danger. They're on the front line of where infections normally show up, so they are expressing a whole bunch of different receptors that will recognize different PAMPs and DAMPs. Now, these receptors that recognize a PAMP or a DAMP, they are pattern recognition receptors or PRRs, and essentially, each PRR is specialized to recognize a particular DAMP or PAMP.

blocks.label: Selection criteria for PAMPs and distinguishing self from non-self
blocks.why: The lecturer outlines the evolutionary requirements for effective pathogen-associated molecular patterns across bacteria, viruses, and eukaryotic pathogens.
blocks.content: So what makes a good PAMP? We want to have a product that is made by a microbe, but not all products made by microbes are equal. If there is a product that's only made by one particular Subspecies of E. coli, and is not made by any other bacteria, that's not going to be a particularly useful PAMP. Okay? We ideally want it to be shared by broad classes of pathogens, because we've got a limited number of these pattern recognition receptors to go around, and so the more different pathogens that can be recognized by a single receptor, the better. Now, ideally, we want it to be essential for the survival of the pathogen. We want the product that's being recognized to be critical for that pathogen. Because, again, if this was just a random protein that was being made by E. coli, and an E. coli doesn't really need that protein, if that protein is what's triggering the immune system, E. coli will just stop making it. Right? Whereas if it is essential for the life of E. coli, E. coli doesn't have the option to not make the protein anymore. So what we tend to have are PAMPs that are selected are ones that are essential for the survival of the organism and highly conserved. Okay? Highly conserved is another way of saying that they're essential, because it means that as species have diverged, they've kept this particular molecule intact, identical, because it has a critical function. Now, at the same time, there are plenty of products that would match this criteria that are not good as PAMPs, and that's because they are so conserved that they are present in the vertebrate host and in bacteria. Now, that doesn't do us any good at all. If we are recognizing a basic component of cell membranes that is present in bacteria and in our own cells, essentially, we're just going to get signaled constantly, so it's going to be useless. So we need to have molecules that are absent from the vertebrate host. This is generally pretty easy with bacteria. It becomes a lot harder with parasites and yeast, with eukaryotic pathogens, because we share so much more with eukaryotic pathogens than we do with prokaryotic pathogens. And essentially, this system will now enable the innate immune system to distinguish self from non-self. And I thought I'd just mention these terms here because you're going to hear them over and again in immunology. Self refers to everything that is part of ourselves, everything that is one of our cells, human cell, or a product of a human cell, that is self. Non-self is everything else. Yeah. That will include pathogens, but it will also include commensal organisms. It will include harmless stuff like pollen, food that we eat. Okay? Anything that our body is exposed to that's not actually made by human cells is non-self. And so we want these PAMPs to distinguish self from non-self and then ideally pathogenic non-self from non-pathogenic non-self. So the type of products that end up being good PAMPs, in bacteria, they'll tend to be components of the cell wall, components of the cell membrane. They are highly conserved within bacteria, but they're highly different from bacteria to vertebrates. In the viruses, they tend to be coat proteins and in particular, nucleic acids. The genome of a virus is quite different from the genome of vertebrates. And then, as I said before, parasites and yeast are more difficult because there are fewer non-conserved PAMPs that are eligible. And there are a few like DPI anchors that are expressed at higher levels in parasites than they are in humans.

blocks.label: Pattern recognition receptor genetics and cellular localization
blocks.why: The lecturer describes how pattern recognition receptors are germline encoded and positioned in specific cellular compartments to detect pathogens.
blocks.content: So the pattern recognition receptors, these are what detect the PAMPs and the DAMPs. A few key points to make here. The first one is that these are germline encoded. This means that they are hardwired. The sequence of the receptor is embedded in our genome. Now, that does not sound particularly profound because in fact, almost everything that we've got is germline encoded. The only reason worth mentioning it now is that there are two genes that are exceptions to being germline encoded, and it happens to be the T cell receptor and the B cell receptor, which are the systems that are used for the adaptive immune response. So the adaptive immune response is not germline encoded, which is very, very strange. The pattern recognition receptors, they are all germline encoded just like classical genes. They're present in our genome, and that means that if we've got a gene that recognizes a component of bacterial cell wall, that gene has to evolve with us over generations, unlike the adaptive immune system where it can evolve in minutes. The other thing that's worth mentioning is that when they get expressed, these pathogen recognition receptors, they have to be present in the right part of the cell to correspond for where that type of pathogen is likely to turn up. So if you have got a PRR that is meant to be recognizing a viral genome, that is a very useful thing for you to have in the cytosol of the cell, where the viral genomes will be let loose, and they have to be released into the cytosol, so they can have access to ribosomes to make their proteins and everything. And so that's where you want the pathogen recognition receptors for viral genomes to be in the cytosol of the cell. On the other hand, if you've got something that's going to recognize the flagellum of a extracellular bacteria, then you want to have that present on the surface of the cell so that you can detect any bacteria that are swimming past and tell the cell about these bacteria that are present in the extracellular compartment. And then the endosome is an interesting compartment. It is walled off from-- well, it's encapsulated by a membrane from the cytosol, and it's a sampling of material from the surface. And so that you'll sometimes have different pattern recognition receptors present in the endosome.

blocks.label: Toll-like receptors and intracellular signaling pathways
blocks.why: The lecturer details the structure, localization, and transcriptional signaling pathways of Toll-like receptors.
blocks.content: Now, the most important class of PRRs, and the class that you'll hear about most often, are the toll-like receptors or TLRs. The toll-like receptors, they are named this because they are related to the receptor toll found in Drosophila. If you're not used to Drosophila, they are fruit fly, tiny little flies that are commonly used as research organisms. There's a picture of a Drosophila on here. Over to the right, you can see the head and the eye, and to the left, you got wings and ears. Sorry, wings and legs. And then the thorax is that very hairy-looking bit in the middle. Now, those are not hairs. This particular Drosophila is a knockout for the gene toll, which is sensing microbial infection and drives the production of antimicrobial peptides. And because it is a knockout for toll, that Drosophila has got fungus infection to the extent where the entire Drosophila is just riddled with fungus, and you've got all the hyphae that are now bursting out of that thorax to the point where it looks like it's a hairy fly. Those are all fungal hyphae that are bursting out because it's just immunodeficient. It can't sense the presence of an infection. So even though it's got the ability to produce all of these great antimicrobials, it doesn't because it doesn't have the ability to sense the infection. Okay? This is how important recognition is. It doesn't matter if you have the ability if you can't actually turn it on at will.

blocks.label: human toll-like receptor family, ligands, and localization
blocks.why: it details the general properties, ligand specificities, structure, and cellular locations of human TLRs
blocks.content: Now, in humans, we have 10 TLRs. These are functionally, they work quite differently from the Drosophila toll, but they are similar in that they have got some sequence preservation, and that they are recognizing features that are PAMPs, so they're typical features from bacteria, fungi, viruses, and parasites. Now they're going to activate downstream transcription factors. They're receptors that activate transcription factors. That's their job. And then just to make a point that the toll-like receptors that tend to recognize bacterial products, they're going to be driving the particular types of immune responses that are very good at dealing with bacteria, like pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines. Remember, chemokines are chemotactic cytokines that pull in inflammatory cells. While the pattern recognition receptors that recognize viral nucleic acids, these are going to be much more likely to stimulate interferons. So interferons are a great mechanism by which cells tell cells to basically shore up their own defenses, and a interferon-exposed cell puts in place cellular mechanisms that make it hard for a virus to proliferate. So these are the 10 toll-like receptors present in humans, slightly different in mice and other species. Each of these can recognize different classes of ligands from different microbes. I think the most important one for you to remember is toll-like receptor four. This is because it is the most potent of the toll-like receptors, and when it binds lipopolysaccharide or LPS, which is a product in the outer membrane of gram-negative bacteria, it is extremely potent at activating the immune system. Even really trace amounts of endotoxin or LPS are able to activate many different cell types in the immune system. So some things about TLRs. They can be homodimers or heterodimers. Homodimers meaning two copies of the protein that are binding together and working together. Heterodimer meaning two different proteins that are binding together and working together. They can be located at the plasma membrane or in endosomes. They are transmembrane proteins, so they work when they're in a membrane, but they don't just have to be sensing the outside material by being at the plasma membrane. They can also sense material that is internalized by being present inside endosomes. They tend to be detecting microbial proteins, carbohydrates, and lipoproteins. We have other systems in place that are better at detecting nucleic acids, although they can detect nucleic acids as well, especially the ones that are present in endosomes.

blocks.label: toll-like receptor downstream signaling mechanisms and spatial logic
blocks.why: it explains how TLR signal transduction works, how surface versus endosomal localization determines signaling outcomes, and how TLR signaling synergizes with stress pathways
blocks.content: Now, when it comes to the signaling system, the signaling of toll-like receptors, the signaling of many immune pathways is actually really important. The reason being that these are often very druggable targets, and if you want to be able to activate the immune system or dampen the immune system, understanding how the signaling pathway works lets you design drugs that can interrupt the signal transmission. And if you interrupt the signal transmission, you interrupt the effect of that signal. Now, that said, I don't expect you to learn the signaling pathways. At this point, it is fine for you to think of the way the signaling works is that you've got the receptors on the surface, then you've got a black box where that binding event is just transmitted to the nucleus And the nucleus signal is going to be the activation of transcription factors, and the transcription factors will activate the downstream genes. Okay? And that's enough for you to have here. Now, what I do want to mention is that you can see that we've got on the surface here different TLRs. They are sensing different products, but they are converging on a similar signaling pathway. Okay? So they're going to activate the similar sets of genes. So whether or not you have activation of TLR5 or TLR4, you get a very similar cellular response because you're activating that same transcriptional pathway. On the other hand, the TLRs that are present on an endosome, they are using different signaling mediators, so they're activating a different signaling cascade, which leads to different transcription factors and different response genes. And so this is why the TLRs that are present on the surface are going to be activating pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines that are particularly good at dealing with extracellular bacteria, while the ones that are present on the endosomes are going to be activating interferons that are very good at dealing with either viruses or intracellular bacteria because the location of where that signal is being given is extra information. Okay? It's useful for the immune system to know, one, we've got an infection, and two, the infection is intracellular or extracellular. So that information comes from where that signal is being received. Now, you can see the interesting case of TLR4, where TLR4 is linked up to different signaling pathways when it's on the plasma membrane versus when it's been endocytosed. So the same receptor will give you a different signal depending on if it's engaged at the surface or if it's engaged in the endosome, because the cell needs to know where that signal is arising so it can activate the appropriate immune response. Now, the other thing that I'll mention here, and I don't expect people to have picked it up, but if we look on this pathway, we're seeing a lot of the same types of genes involved in signaling, like MKKs and p38, JNK, AP-1. A lot of these signaling molecules and transcription factors are the same signaling molecules and the same transcription factors that I mentioned a few lectures ago in terms of cellular stress. That the stressed cell was activating these pathways, and now you're seeing the same pathways being activated by the infected cell. And actually, infection and stress, they are converging and synergizing. Those signals are acting together. A little bit of stress doesn't do much. A little bit of infection doesn't do much. A little bit of stress plus a little bit of infection really triggers a strong reaction from the cell because of those synergies.

blocks.label: Cytoplasmic PRRs and the inflammasome pathway
blocks.why: The lecturer discusses intracellular receptor families and the assembly of the inflammasome to activate interleukin-1 beta.
blocks.content: Now, toll-like receptors are very important, but they're not the only family of pattern recognition receptors. We're going to touch on some other families. One of them is the C-type lectins, CLRs. They're important in fungal infections. The RIG-I-like receptors, these are quite important for detecting viral RNA in the cytoplasm. The Nod-like receptors, or NLRs, these are really quite important in a number of different diseases. These are cytoplasmic receptors. They're able to recognize both PAMPs and DAMPs. One of the most important of these receptors is Nod-2. This recognizes muramyl dipeptide, which is a component of the cell wall of most bacteria. And actually, the recognition of bacteria by Nod-2 drives some of the phenotype of Crohn's disease, which is a type of inflammatory bowel disease. So this indicates how these pathways that sense infection can be linked up to inflammatory disease because that process of sensing bacterial products activates the inflammatory cascade, which is sometimes beneficial and sometimes detrimental.

blocks.label: The inflammasome pathway and its activation of IL-1 beta
blocks.why: The lecturer explains the assembly of the inflammasome complex, how it activates caspase-1 to process IL-1 beta, and how DAMPs trigger it in chronic disease.
blocks.content: Now, another key pathway is the inflammasome pathway. These are a large multi-protein structure that can form inside cells. They're made up of the sensing molecules like NALP3 or NLRP3, and what they can do is they can form this cytosolic inflammasome structure. So just zooming in on this structure in a bit more detail, you've got all of these different forms of something like NLRP3. They are coming together and concatenating in the presence of a signal. So if they're recognizing something, they all concatenate on it. They form these long fibers. Those fibers are then assembled into this pinwheel structure by ASC spec and caspase-1, and what that does is it converts caspase-1 into the active form of the protein. Now, this becomes quite important because activated caspase-1 is a protease, and what it does is it takes a number of different inflammatory cytokines that are produced in an inactive form, and it converts them into an active form. The key example of this is interleukin1-beta. This is a highly inflammatory cytokine, and it's got a lot of safety features built into this cytokine. One of which is the fact that it's always made as a pro form, which is inactive because it's got this inactivating peptide stuck onto it. For IL-1B to be activated, you need the inflammasome to form, and then that will clip off IL-1 beta The propeptide creating the mature IL-1 beta peptide, which leads to inflammation. Now, this means that to get good IL-1 beta, you need to have multiple different signals. You need to have some signals from toll-like receptors saying you should produce IL-1 beta, and then you have to have other signals from the inflammasome saying you have to mature IL-1 beta. So multiple safety signals means that you've got a way of escalating the immune system. You can produce a bunch of different cytokines. Some of them are weakly inflammatory, but they're turned on automatically. Others are highly inflammatory, but they're made in an inactivated state, and only if you have extra danger signals coming in do you activate those highly inflammatory cytokines. Now, unfortunately, from our perspective, these are not only activated by infectious molecules, they're also activated by DAMPs, these damage-associated molecular patterns, and DAMPs can form in the complete absence of an infection. So we have examples of cholesterol crystals, crystals in gout, stressed proteins in diabetes, that are all able to activate the inflammasome because of the damage and stress that's going on to cells. And then once the inflammasome is activated, we get a situation where we're now driving inflammation, and then we get this cycle where the inflammation causes stress, the stress causes inflammation, and you end up with a chronic inflammatory disease like we were talking about in that first lecture.

blocks.label: Sentinel cells: mast cells and macrophages
blocks.why: The lecturer explains how mast cells and macrophages sense danger and mediate local and systemic inflammatory responses.
blocks.content: Now, the key cells that activate are the sentinel cells. We'll just go to one example of a sentinel cell here, which is a mast cell, and we were talking about mast cells in the last lecture. That we've got the ability to sense multiple different sources of information saying that there's a potential infection, and if they see that, they'll release these preformed granules. And so here we can talk now about the actual molecules that are being sensed will be different PAMPs, like LPS, signaling through different pattern recognition receptors like TLR4, and then that signal is what drives the release of these preformed granules. Okay? And we'll learn about these other signals that are present on there, like IgE and complement three A and five A in later lectures. Macrophages are probably the best sentinel cell. They have a very wide range of receptors so that they are versatile in detecting different types of infection. They're probably the prototype of an immune cell that is present. So evolutionarily speaking, we probably had macrophages before any other immune cell, and they have a lot of these primordial functions that are all together. They're not great at anything, but they're good at everything, if that makes sense. And then they're going to be able to send off signals. A lot of these signals are going to have very local effects on the immune system directly around the site of infection, so they're going to be signals to cells saying, "Watch out, there's an infection." They're going to be recruiting cells coming in. It's recruiting cells to the site of infection. But there's also systemic effects. So the effect of some of these cytokines becomes more long range, especially if the concentration of these mediators builds up. So having 10 activated macrophages will give you a very localized inflammation. Having 10,000 activated macrophages gives you enough signal that you get activation at very distal sites, and then that is going to give you systemic effects like fever, shock, any of these sickness-associated behaviors that you'd be used to. These are all happening from cytokines like TNF, IL-6, and IL-1 beta reaching a critical threshold and going across and activating pathways in your brain.

blocks.label: Leukocyte recruitment and extravasation into tissues
blocks.why: The lecturer describes the multi-step process of leukocyte rolling, adhesion, extravasation, and chemokine-directed migration.
blocks.content: Now, one of the effects of the immediate inflammation response is to recruit leukocytes to the site of inflammation, and so we talked last week about how you're going to have this influx of cells coming into the tissue. I just want to spend a couple of slides talking about how this actually happens. The first thing is that you have to work out what cells you want to recruit. Okay? So depending on the types of signal you're going to get, you're going to be sending up different flags, and those different flags will retract different types of immune cells. Now, the cell type that puts up the flag is the endothelial cell. These are the cells that line the blood vessels, and essentially, the endothelial cells are being told by cells inside the tissue, "We need more neutrophils. Recruit more neutrophils." Okay? So they're getting a signal in the form of cytokines, and their job is to take that signal and then put up another signal in the form of these flags to recruit the cells that are needed in the tissue. Now, these flags are adhesion molecules. They tend to be selectins and integrins and molecules from the immunoglobulin superfamily. Now, I just want to make one mention of this, because you'll often hear about immunoglobulin superfamily, and you might be thinking that this has something to do with antibody, because antibody is immunoglobulin. It's not. It's just that they have got a structural relationship. It's in the same family of proteins, but this is not actually to do with antibody at all. This is just molecules that have got some structural similarity with one of the folds in antibody. So you can just think of it as a separate phenomenon. So the cells are going to be present in our blood, and most of the key cells we're talking about here are going to always be present in our blood, and they're circulating. They're going around and around in our blood. They're waiting for some flags to go up for those cells to then enter the tissue. Now, blood is really fast. It is pumping around our body. Blood will do a full circuit of our body in about eight minutes, and the cells are really moving at the speed of millimeters per second. Now, that doesn't sound particularly fast until you think about how small a cell is, and in effect, these cells are moving at something like 300 cell diameters per second. This is faster than the top speed of a Formula 1 racing car. Yeah. So this is the type of speed that these cells are moving at inside the blood. If they were to be stopped suddenly, they would be ripped in pieces, okay? If they just hit a flag and then immediately ground to halt, most of the cell body would still be flying down the blood, and there'd just be a little bit of the cell membrane stuck onto the flag. So it's a process of slowing down. There are particular parts of the body that are good at slowing down cells. This tends to happen in the postcapillary venules. So you've got your major arteries going into the capillary bed, and then they're going to turn into the veins that are leaving the capillary bed. That point where you go from the capillaries into the veins, that is where the blood slows down enough that the cells can start to do these type of interactions, and the first thing is a rolling interaction. So this is not a hard stop. This is just almost like rolling down some Velcro. The cells are just slowing down, that very weak tethering to get the cell to start tumbling it down the endothelial wall so it can slow down. And then once it's slowed down enough, these molecules that do tight binding become more important, and this is what actually brings the cell to a stop. So these will be key molecules like ICAM, LFA-1, that will bring the cell to a complete stop at that location. Now, once that cell has stopped, it can extravasate. So extravasation is the process of going from the blood into the tissue. Now, there are different ways it can do this. It can find the spot that is between two endothelial cells, and it can basically unzip the contact between those two endothelial cells and squeeze through. Cells are very squishy. Immune cells are very good at squeezing through. Essentially, this looks like, when you image it, a very floofy cat going through a very small cat flap, right? They're just shrinking down to what you think is impossibly small and then puffing out on the other side. T cells in particular, they don't even need to go between cells. They can actually dive straight through a cell. They can go through that plasma membrane, make a very small hole, squeeze in, swim across the cell, pop out the other side. They're very good at translocating these surfaces. It's what immune cells do. Now, once you're inside the tissue, that's not it. You have to get to the right part of the tissue, especially considering this, remember, it's all happening after the capillary bed. So if the infection is pre-capillary bed, that cell now has to get to the right spot of the infection, and this is where the chemokines come in, or other chemotactic factors. And these form a gradient where the concentration is very high at the source of the infection, and it is a lower gradient as you go away from the infection. And essentially, for a immune cell to get to the right spot, all it has to do is follow the chemokines and go in the direction where the chemokines are stronger. And if it just keeps on following that pathway, it'll end up in the place where the source of the infection is. Now, neutrophils are able to do this process very quickly. They happen to get in in the very first hours. They're responding to the first flags like ICAM-1. If you've got a defect in neutrophil adhesion to ICAM-1, so an LFA-1 defect, that is going to mean that you've got plenty of neutrophils, but they're not going into the tissues early enough. That means that if you have a bacterial infection, it can turn into a long-term, destructive, we talk about flesh-eating bacteria. This is what will happen, because if you don't have neutrophils coming in, and as a genetic disorder, you'll have kids that are quite healthy until they get the wrong infection, and then they can't deal with that, and so they'll end up having to have amputations and then die, usually quite early in childbirth. Even though they've got all of the right cells, they're just not getting into the tissue, so they can't deal with skin infections. Monocytes come a bit later. They use different flags. You might pick up some of these molecules. It doesn't matter a whole lot at this stage. So what we've just done here is put some molecular detail on this figure that I've been showing the whole time through here. Right? You've got the infection that is breaking through the skin barrier. Now we are talking about not just the infection breaking through, but particular structural features of those microbes, the pathogen-associated molecular patterns. Those are now present together with the microbes. They're being recognized by the sentinel cells through receptors like TLR4 and other pattern recognition receptors. They're sending a signal to the endothelial cells to put up the particular flags that will cause cells to start rolling along the tissue bed here, extravasate, and follow chemokine migration gradients to the site of infection. So it's exactly the same concepts that I've been talking about for a few lectures, but now we've got some of that molecular detail showing how the system is controlled.

blocks.label: Lymphatic drainage and priming adaptive immunity
blocks.why: The lecturer explains how dendritic cells migrate through the lymphatic system to activate adaptive immune responses in lymph nodes.
blocks.content: Now, I do want to mention that we've been talking a lot about what happens at the site of infection, because it's quite important for cells to come in to fight that infection. But once you go into the adaptive immune lectures that are happening shortly, then you realize that it's also important for cells to leave the site of infection. And so here we're talking really about the priming of immune cells for the adaptive immune response to give you good B cells and T cells, gives you good memory. Now, the way this works is that some of these sentinel cells, in particular the dendritic cells, when they get activated and they see infection, they're going to take those antigens, take the signs of infection, and rather than locally stimulate cells, they're going to move through the lymphatic system to a lymph node, and there they're going to distally activate cells, in particular the T cells and B cells. Now, if you're not familiar with lymph and lymph nodes, essentially we've got two systems for circulating fluid around our body. We've got the cardiovascular system, which circulates blood. The purpose of blood is to carry oxygen. Now, when the blood is going through tissues, we want to just give over nutrients and oxygen. But no system is perfect. All systems are leaky. So some of that blood, the fluid in that blood is going to leak into the tissue. So the tissue ends up becoming quite full of liquid, and we've got this extra tissue juice that we need to get back into the blood, and the way we do that is having the lymphatic system, which drains all of that extra juice from the tissues, and it will basically drain it and put it back into the blood. Now, this is set up to have one long series of drainage that all joins up going through lymph nodes so that any of that drainage can be screened for any infections in those lymph nodes. And so we've taken a system that is really just about fluid balance, and then we've put lymph nodes on there to allow us to screen for infections in the tissues that are being drained.

blocks.label: Excessive systemic inflammation and septic shock
blocks.why: The lecturer discusses the pathological consequences of uncontrolled systemic cytokine release leading to septic shock.
blocks.content: Now, the other thing to mention here is we've largely been talking about the activation of the immune system as a positive thing, because generally it is positive. And if we talk about something like local inflammation, it is very useful for us to have blood clotting, cells coming in, being activated, damaging products being formed. We do want to have vasodilation at a local level. But the problem is that when these processes become too severely activated, they can actually be highly detrimental to us. And so, in particular, if we get too much interferon alpha produced, this is one of those pro-inflammatory cytokines, then we can get what is called septic shock and septic shock syndrome. This happens because we've got too much stimulation of TNF production, so too much different exposure to PAMPs. Often it will happen after, say, a burn, and you've got many different infections all happening at the same time. They're all producing TNF. The immune system is just screaming out, and then that's going to cause systemic vasodilation and loss of blood pressure. At that point, you've got septic shock, and you have all of these cardiovascular symptoms that we're going to talk about in a later lecture. This is really quite severe. If you have sepsis, the death rate is 40%. If that's septic shock, that's a death rate of 60%, and that's even in a top-level hospital with round-the-clock care. This is a very serious problem still. And even when you survive, 25% of the sufferers have permanent life-changing effects. It's about 250,000 cases of sepsis a year. It's one of our big unsolved problems in terms of how do we shut off the immune system quickly enough to deal with the septic shock.

blocks.label: Passive and active mechanisms for resolving inflammation
blocks.why: The lecturer details how inflammation is shut down through mediator decay, lipid mediator switching, and anti-inflammatory cytokines.
blocks.content: So this brings us to the final slides of the lecture, which is about resolution of inflammation and repair after inflammation. Now, there are really two major ways in which we're going to shut down the immune system, and this is through passive means and through active means. If you are driving a car and you want to slow down the car, again, you have two different systems. You can have passive systems, so you can just take your foot off the accelerator, and if you take your foot off the accelerator, the car will naturally go to a stop because you've stopped activating it. Or you can actively use the brake. So that's an active system where you are telling the car to stop, and the same is true in the immune system. The passive systems are essentially to remove the production of inflammatory stimuli or get rid of them, while the active stop systems are systems that are really telling the immune system to stop now. So in terms of the passive, many of these mediators have very short half-lives. They are Engineered to have short half-lives because they're signaling molecules. You want them to only last for minutes or hours because you don't want to have an inflammatory molecule that has its effect that lasts for a month, right? Because we're dealing with short-term problems, so we want to have short-term mediators. Many of the cell types are also very short-lived, will die a few hours later. So if you stop recruiting them, then the problem's going to disappear by itself within hours or days. Now, we also have these active stop signals. One of these that's quite important is the shift of macrophages from producing pro-inflammatory lipids to anti-inflammatory lipids. There's also a lipid mediator class switch, where some of these lipids, like prostaglandins and leukotrienes, they've got a series of metabolic enzymes that are creating them, and some of those products are inflammatory, but also some of the products are anti-inflammatory. And if you switch the enzyme at a key step, then those precursors are made into anti-inflammatory products. So these cells can very quickly switch from being pro-inflammatory to anti-inflammatory. And then we have actual cytokines where the product is always made to be anti-inflammatory, like IL-10 and TGF-beta. I think it is useful to know, though, that the immune system isn't generally doing a single switch. It doesn't go from having its foot flat on the accelerator to its foot flat on the brake. Instead, what it does is once it starts up an immune response, it's going to put its foot on the accelerator and a little bit on the brake, and then it's going to slowly lift its foot off the accelerator and slowly put its foot further down on the brake. And so it's really about the balance of activation and inactivation rather than a complete switch from one to the other.

blocks.label: Granulation tissue repair and chronic inflammation
blocks.why: The lecturer explains tissue remodeling by fibroblasts and M2 macrophages alongside causes of chronic inflammation and inflammaging.
blocks.content: Now, just the final point I want to talk about is injury repair. And so this is what's called granulation tissue. So this is tissue that has been inflamed, it has been damaged, and now the body is trying to replace that damaged tissue with healthy tissue. Young bodies are very good at this process. Old bodies are very bad at this process. This is one of the parts of aging, and it works via the process of recruiting fibroblasts. They're going to lay down new extracellular matrix, which is really that scaffolding that holds the cells together into a tissue. You can think of this as sort of the mortar in a brick wall is your extracellular matrix. You need to make new blood vessels, so you can recruit endothelial cell precursors to grow new blood vessels, and you can remodel that extracellular matrix. Now, ideally, you're going to remodel it into a matrix that is just as good as the original young matrix. However, it is very difficult to repair a structure in the presence of damage, and so you end up having extracellular matrix that is suboptimal, and that will give you this type of scar tissue, that is not really as strong as good healthy tissue. Now, macrophages are really quite pivotal in this process. We talk about them as inflammatory cells, but remember that there is this M2 program, which is the other side. This is the janitorial function that they have. So they really are a central control hub for the repair stage. They can phagocytose all the dead cells and all the dead rubbish that's around there. They can recruit the fibroblasts and the endothelial cells. They can digest the old matrix so that new matrix can be laid down by those fibroblasts. And in many cases, this is enough. So in an ideal situation, you've got an infection, you've got a short-lived inflammatory response, it gets rid of the infection, you then have a repair process, and it shuts the whole tissue inflammation down, and the tissue is left normal. And that's how it tends to work when you're young. As you get older, there's this process where your body becomes more prone to inflammation. You might have heard of the term inflammaging. Inflammaging is this kind of conversion to a default inflammatory process. And so under this situation, the tissue is not fully restored back to homeostasis. It stays in this situation where there's always just a little bit of inflammation causing a little bit of damage, which causes a little bit of inflammation. And this can happen for a number of different reasons. So it might be that the cause of the inflammation is something completely endogenous. So if you've got a stomach ulcer, you're going to be producing stomach acid. That acid through the ulcer is going to be damaging the tissue, so you're always causing a bit of damage, and you can't heal it because it becomes self-perpetuating. It could also be an agent that is non-degradable, so silica, dust particles, things like asbestos. The reason why asbestos is bad in our lungs is because when it gets in our lungs, it can cause a little bit of irritation, and we can't degrade it. It'll stay there for our lifetime, just constantly causing irritation, cause inflammation, and you get this low-grade inflammation that's going to be damaging. It can also be infectious agents that we never get rid of, so things like mycobacterium tuberculosis are very hard to clear completely, and so we always have that bit of infection, and so we don't get rid of it. Or it might be autoimmunity, where we're attacking components of our body, where our immune system is now mistakenly thinking that part of our body is an infection and tries to clear it. And so under that type of condition, we get these inflamed reactions going on.

blocks.label: Granuloma formation as an evolved pathogen containment strategy
blocks.why: The lecturer describes how the immune system uses granulomas to wall off persistent infections like tuberculosis.
blocks.content: And then just the last slide I want to point out is that sometimes these chronic inflammatory reactions, most times they're bad. We don't want to have chronic inflammation. But we shouldn't forget that most of the processes that we have, we have evolved because they are sometimes beneficial. And we look at the situations where these processes go wrong and are maladaption, but they have evolved so that we have them as a useful process. And here we can think about something like tuberculosis. So tuberculosis is a infection by a bacteria, Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It lives inside cells. It can proliferate inside cells. It is very hard for a body to get rid of a tuberculosis infection. It is fantastic at hiding inside our cells. If you try to destroy all of the Mycobacterium, you end up destroying huge amounts of lung as you're hunting down and killing every infected cell, and ultimately, you're very rarely successful. The body's not good at sterilizing completely Mycobacterium tuberculosis. So the attempt to destroy every last bacterium is going to leave you with no lung capacity, and you're going to die. So it's actually a sensible choice for the immune system to say, "We're not going to try to clear Mycobacterium tuberculosis. We're going to try to control it. We're going to keep it under limits." And one of the ways it can do this is form a granuloma, which is basically to wall off part of the tissue and say, "Within this wall, that infection can run rampant, and we're not going to control it. But we're going to stop any infection leaving that zone." Okay? Now, we often talk about this as if it's something that is made by tuberculosis, and in fact, tuberculosis does drive this reaction to happen. And we can talk about tuberculosis has evolved to exploit this granuloma loophole so that it can hide out in the body long-term. But the process does not require a microbe to start, and in fact, there are mutations in NOD2 that make the NOD2 hyperactive and activated without any microbial products. And in those patients, even in the absence of any infection, they will spontaneously form these granulomas. So that tells us that this granuloma formation is beneficial and a programmed response that we use all the time, and that sometimes it goes wrong, and sometimes it allows infections to hide out.

blocks.content: Okay, that's it for me. Next lecture is complements.
